[BODY] Now they wake up: it had been better to have kept awake. They see the evil growth, though they did not see the evil sowing. Overwhelmed with the sight of the spoiled field, they hastened to tell their lord, wondering much how such a state of things could have come about. What a question to ask of their master: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Whence hath it tares?</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>They were sure that he sowed “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">good seed</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>and nothing else; and they evidently thought that he would know who sowed the bastard wheat. We, too, wonder how so much evil can have entered into a region wherein Christ has set his ministers, and we cry out in astonishment, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">From whence then hath it tares?</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>The question is best left with the Master; but the asking it is a confession that we have been asleep.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">28.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up?</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">The householder  </sty>had not slept. He knew who had done the cruel wrong. He who is the enemy of God and man, and he only, had perpetrated this piece of malice. It may have seemed to be a learned doctor, or a clever poet, or a treacherous orator, who scattered doubt among the people, and introduced skeptics into the church; but the worker behind the scenes, the real author of the mischief, is always the devil himself.

[BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">The servants  </sty>were eager to undo the mischief at once in the first way that suggested itself. Out with the false wheat, and let the true wheat grow! A thing more easy to propose than to do; but one which would naturally occur to all true servants who were sorry for their neglect, and eager to set matters right. Had there been weeds in the corn, the hoe could have removed them; but this darnel grew on the wheat, and was like the wheat, and thus was the true picture of those in the church and in the world, who are nominal Christians, and fair moralists, but who know nothing of the life of God. We cannot get rid of these, and yet how often we wish we could!

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">29.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.</sty>

--- PAGE 209 ---

[BODY] The darnel was so plentiful, had become so intermixed with the corn, and was so much like it, that it would not be possible to cut up the one without pulling up the other also. In fact, there was a false wheat which grew upon the true corn, and to part these would be perilous to the crop. Hasty disciplinarians have often cast out the best and retained the worst. Where evil is clear and open, we may not hesitate to deal with it; but where it is questionable, we had better hold our hand till we have fuller guidance.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">30.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.</sty>

[BODY] Suffer the two seeds to remain together for a season, that they may be the more effectually separated later on. It is true the evil will hinder and hamper the good; but even this will be better than that you should cast out the good by mistake. A separation time will come, and that will be “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">in the time of harvest</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>when both will be fully developed. That will be a fit season, when the division can be made and no harm done thereby <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">The reapers  </sty>then employed will do the work correctly, efficiently, universally, and finally. For the false wheat there will be burning in bundles; for the true, ingathering into the Lord’s own storehouse. This will be a perfect separation, and we are bidden to wait for it. Our Lord’s “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">I will say to the reapers</sty>” may very well keep us from making any hasty speeches to the elders of the churches, or to the magistrates of the land, so as to excite them to hurried and ungenerous discipline. Thorns and thistles they can root up, but the darnel is another matter. Magistrates and churches may remove the openly wicked from their society; the outwardly good who are inwardly worthless they must leave; for the judging of hearts is beyond their sphere.

[BODY] Our Lord declares that the doom of the false wheat, the bastard professors, is terrible. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Bind them in bundles;  </sty>put<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>like with like, sinner with like sinner. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">To burn them.  </sty>No words can be more suggestive of terrible destruction After this what a quiet, peaceful tone we hear in the words, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Gather the wheat into my barn.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>All gathered, all recognized as

--- PAGE 210 ---

[BODY] the Lord’s own, all housed in his storehouse.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">31, 32.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">  Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Mustard seed is the least of all seeds  </sty>in proportion to that which comes of it; but it has a peculiar life in it, and therefore it produces so great a growth. The man in the parable we know: his field is the church, or the heart; he <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">takes  </sty>the seed which, perhaps, others neglect because they think it so small; he sows the living seed in his own field, and watches over it. The work of grace in the church and in the individual, is so apparent, that persons who know as little about heavenly things as linnets and sparrows, come and find shelter beneath the holy and beneficent influences and institutions which are its outgrowth.

[BODY] We could not have guessed that our Lord and his twelve apostles would produce the myriad churches of Christendom. We cannot even now tell whereto a humble effort to do good may grow. If the Lord has planted the incorruptible seed within, its destiny is a great one.

[BODY] Good Master, hasten this blessed development. We have seen nearly enough of the mustard seed; now let us see the tree.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">33.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.</sty>

[BODY] Many expositors argue that this relates to the power of evil in the church,

--- PAGE 212 ---

[BODY] or in the heart. On this interpretation we see why “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">a woman took</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>the leaven, and why she was so secret about it, that it is said she hid it<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">.</sty> According to the rule which is observed in the use of this symbol, leaven must be taken as the type of evil; and if the rule must be applied in this case, the teaching is obvious and valuable. [BODY] But the connection does not lead us so to interpret. Is not leaven here used simply as another picture of an influence which appears feeble, but turns out to be active, conquering, and at length all-pervading? This, though hidden in obscurity, in the midst of nations comparable to “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">three measures of meal</sty>”, wrought with a mysterious rapidity, and will still continue to work in the whole mass of the world, and subdue the nations to itself. Let our friends take their choice of the two interpretations, and learn a good lesson from either or both. From evil leaven, the Lord preserve us; by holy influences may we all be wrought upon!

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">34, 35.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">  All these things spake Jesus unto the multitude in parables; and without a parable spake he not unto them: that; it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying, I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things which have been kept secret from the foundation of the world.</sty>

[BODY] That prophet was David, or Asaph. The Psalm (78.) begins, “Give ear, O my people, to my law.” By whom could this be spoken but by God? and yet in the third verse this same person speaks of “our fathers”; and therefore he must be a man. Here, then, in this seventy-eighth psalm, is the sacred person who is both God and man, and to our Lord Jesus Christ the language is most fitly applied by the evangelist. Our Lord speaks hidden

--- PAGE 213 ---

[BODY] things, and sets forth <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">secret  </sty>things in an open parable, which is understood by those who have had the eyes of their understanding opened, while those who are self-blinded perceive not his meaning. These parables contain ancient secrets and deep mysteries; and, may be, there is more of prophecy in them than we have yet perceived.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">36.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then Jesus sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field.</sty>

[BODY] Possibly, they had made out the mustard seed and the leaven, but the <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">tares</sty> remained a puzzle to them. We are not sorry for this, since, through their ignorance, we obtain our Lord’s own interpretation. We should certainly have missed our way without it.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">37.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man.</sty>

[BODY] He came to this world on purpose to sow the kingdom of heaven in it. All the grace, and truth, and spiritual life among us is<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>of his sowing.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">38.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">The field is the world,  </sty>including the church; but the field is not the church exclusively: for “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the good seed</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>or “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the children of the kingdom</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>is<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>much the same as the church, and the evil seed are persons who mingle with the people of God, and live together with them in necessary association in the great field of the world. Churchfellowship is not particularly aimed at, though it is encompassed by the terms used. Bigots have tried to extirpate heretics, and national churches have even forbidden unsound thinkers to remain in the country; but all attempts at securing any region from having infidels or heretics residing in it have soured into persecution. Nowhere on earth can we maintain a settlement of saints alone. In many cases, the cruel treatment of the very best of men has been produced by the notion that they were erroneous teachers, and therefore ought not to be tolerated. To contend earnestly against error by

As if it were a dainty dish for her tooth, the prophet’s head must be served up in <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">a charger.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">9.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them, which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her.</sty>

[BODY] Pretty sorrow! A crocodile is said to shed tears over those it snaps in two. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">The King</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>was afraid of the consequences. Poor king! He may have felt a dying struggle of conscience, for Herod had some sort of reverence for John; yet his grief could not have been very deep, for he had already willed to kill him. The king feared that his courtiers and comrades at the drinking bout would think him weak, and perhaps jeer at him for being too religious to touch a prophet. Such fear of being thought weak proved that he was weak indeed. In addition to this, Herodias would consider him to be by no means so fond of her as he had professed to be, and how could he endure her passionate grief? Moreover, he was “a man of honor”, and <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">for the oath’s sake  </sty>he must not run back. With the regret which a wolf feels because he must eat the lamb, he gave orders for the murder of John, and the handing of his head to the young girl. Rash promises, and even oaths, are no excuse for doing wrong. The promise was in itself null and void, because no man has a right to promise to do wrong. Wicked oaths ought to be repented of, and not acted out; but this cruel tyrant commanded the murder, and so went through with his horrible promise.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">10. </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And he sent, and beheaded John in the prison.</sty>

[BODY] Herod<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  sent, and beheaded John.  </sty>By<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>word a precious life is ended. How lightly tyrants think of murder! No miracle was wrought for John’s deliverance. Why should there be? It was well for the Baptist to go to his reward, for his work was done. He was not left to pine in solitude: the man of God left his prison for Paradise by one sudden stroke of the sword. It was a foul murder, but to the Baptist it was a happy release. He was no longer in the power of Herod or Herodias: he received his crown in heaven though he had lost his head on earth

--- PAGE 225 ---


[BODY] Herod <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">is  </sty>said to have “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">beheaded John</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">;  </sty>for what he ordered to be done is set to his account, and in his conscience he knew it. We do ourselves what we do by others. Men may sin by proxy, but they will be guilty in person.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">11. </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And his head was brought in a charger, and given to the damsel: and she brought it to her mother.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">12.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And his disciples came, and took up the boy/, and buried it, and went and told Jesus</sty>

[BODY] The good man’s followers did not desert their murdered leader: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">his disciples came.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>The mangled corpse was surrendered to them; they reverently <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">took up the body, and buried it.  </sty>They were his disciples still, and his death was not the death of their faith. But it is not said by the Evangelist that they buried John, but “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">they took up his body, and buried  </sty>it”, not him. [BODY] What remained for John’s disciples but to go to their leader’s Friend and Master, and tell him all the circumstances, and wait further orders? John had taught them well, since they went at once to Jesus when their teacher was dead.

[BODY] When we are in a great trouble, we shall be wise to do our best, and at the same time tell the Lord Jesus all about it, that he may direct us further as

[BODY] to what we are to do. What a relief to tell Jesus! It was a painful story for him to hear; but he would be sure to impart consolation to these mourners; and in our case also he will send comfort.

[CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 14:13-22</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">OUR KING GIVES A GREAT BANQUET</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">13.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">When Jesus heard of it, he departed thence by ship into a desert place apart: and when the people had heard thereof, they followed him on foot out of the cities.</sty>

[BODY] Our Lord could not allow so sad an event as the death of his Forerunner to pass without special devotion; perhaps also he judged it wise to be out of the dominions of Herod just at this time. The discreet use of solitude has yet to be learned by many workers.

[BODY] The multitude would not permit him to be at rest: they were curious, anxious, necessitous; and so they were soon <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">on foot  </sty>after him. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">15.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And when it was evening, his disciples came to him, saying, This is a desert place, and the time is now past; send the multitude away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves victuals.</sty>

[BODY] The disciples had the compassion of men who see the need; but to their human thought there seemed but one poor way out of it, namely, in effect to shirk the difficulty by <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">sending the multitudes away</sty>. The short way out of a perplexity is generally a very poor affair. To this day many Christians get no further than leaving the masses to themselves, or to some unknown influences which may turn up. Christ for Master of the feast: apostles for butlers; thousands for numbers; and miracles for supplies! What a far more glorious feast is that which the gospel spreads for hungry souls! [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">20.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Five thousand men</sty> is no small dinnerparty. Think of five thousand fed with live loaves! A loaf among a thousand! Our King will yet feed all the nations on that gospel which is today so little thought of. Amen! So let it be.

[CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 14:23-26</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">THE KING RULING WINDS AND WAVES</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">23.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And when he had sent the multitudes away, he went up into a mountain apart to pray: and when the evening was come, he was there alone.</sty>

On the lake of Galilee the wind rushes down from the gullies between the mountains, and causes grievous peril to little boats; sometimes fairly lifting them out of the water, and anon submerging them beneath the waves. That deep lake was peculiarly dangerous for small craft. They were far from land, for they were “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">in the midst of the sea</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>equally distant from either shore. [BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">wind was contrary</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>and would not let them go to any place which they sought. It was a whirlwind, and they were whirled about by it, but could not use it for reaching either shore. How much did their case resemble ours when we are in sore distress! We are tossed about, and can do nothing; the blast is too furious for us to bear up against it, or even to live while driven before it.

[BODY] One happy fact remains: Jesus is pleading on the shore though we are struggling on the sea. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">25.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And in the fourth watch of the night Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea</sty>

[BODY] Jesus is sure to come. The night wears on and the darkness thickens; <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the fourth watch of the night  </sty>draws near, but where is he? Faith says, “He must come.” Though he should stay away till almost break of day, he must come. Unbelief asks, “How can he come?” Ah, he will answer for himself: he can make his own way. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Jesus went unto them, walking on the sea.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>He comes in the teeth of the wind, and on the face of the wave. Never fear that he will fail to reach the storm-tossed barque: his love will find out the way. Whether it be to a single disciple, or to the church as a whole, Jesus will appear in his own chosen hour, and his time is sure to be the most timely.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">26.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were troubled, saying, It is a spirit; and they cried out for fear.</sty>

[BODY] Yes, <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the disciples saw him;  </sty>saw<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Jesus their Lord, and derived no comfort from the sight. Poor human nature’s sight is a blind thing compared with the vision of a spiritual faith. They saw, but knew not what they saw. What could it be but a phantom? How could a real man walk on those foaming billows? How could he stand in the teeth of such a hurricane? They were already at their wits’ end, and the apparition put an end to their courage. We seem to hear their shriek of alarm: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">they cried out for fear.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>We read not that “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">they were troubled</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>before: they were

--- PAGE 235 ---

[BODY] old sailors, and had no dread of natural forces; but a <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">spirit  </sty>— ah, that was too much of a terror. They were at their worst now; and yet, if they had known it, they were on the verge of their best. It is noteworthy that the nearer Jesus was the greater was their fear. Want of discernment blinds the soul to its richest consolations. Lord, be near, and let me know thee! Let me not have to say with Jacob, “Surely God was in this place; and I knew it not!”

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">27.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not of afraid.</sty>

[BODY] He did not keep them in suspense: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Straightway Jesus spake unto them.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>How sweetly sounded that loving and majestic voice! [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">28.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And Peter answered him and said, Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Peter  </sty>must<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>be the first to speak; he is impulsive; and besides, he was a sort of foreman in the company. Surely, he wist not what he said. Yet we, too, have put our Lord to tests almost as improper. Have we not said, “If thou hast ever blessed me, give me this and that”? We, too, have had our water-walking, and have ventured where nothing but special grace could uphold us. Lord, what is man?

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">29.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And he said, Come. And when Peter was come down out of the ship he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.</sty>

[BODY] When good men are unwise and presumptuous, it may be for their lasting good to learn their folly by experience. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">He said, Come.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Peter’s Lord is about to teach him a practical lesson. We can do anything if we have divine authorization, and courage enough to take the Lord at his word. Now there were two on the sea, Two wonders! Which was the greater? The render may not find it easy to reply. Let him consider.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">30.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.</sty>

[BODY] “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">But</sty>”: a sorrowful “but” for poor Peter. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">31.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?</sty>

[BODY] Our Lord delays not when our peril is imminent and our cry is urgent: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>He first “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">caught him</sty>” and then taught him. --- PAGE 237 ---

[BODY] must needs do so. When we are saved is the fit time for us to chasten ourselves for our unbelief. Let us learn from our Lord, that we may not reprove others till we have first helped them out of their difficulties.

[BODY] Our doubts are unreasonable: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Wherefore didst thou doubt?</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>If there be reason for little faith, there is evidently reason for great confidence. It looked like great faith when Peter walked the water; but a little wind soon proved it to be “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">little faith.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Till our faith is tried, we can form no reliable estimate of it.

[BODY] After his Lord had taken him by the hand, Peter sank no further, but resumed the walk of faith. How easy to have faith when we are close to Jesus!

[CENTERED] Lord, when our faith fails, come you to us, and we shall walk on the wave.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">32.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And when they were come into the ship, the wind ceased.</sty>

[BODY] So that Peter’s walk and his rescue had happened in the face of the tempest. He could walk the water well enough when his Lord held his hand, and so can we. What a sight! Jesus and Peter, hand in hand, walking upon the sea! The two made for the ship at once: miracles are never spun out to undue length. Was not Peter glad to leave the tumultuous element, and at the same time to perceive that the gale was over? “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">When they were come into the ship, the wind ceased</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">;  </sty>it is well to be safe in a storm, but more pleasant to find the calm return and the hurricane end. How gladly did the disciples welcome their Lord, and their brother, Peter, who though wet to the skin, was a wiser man for his adventure!

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">33.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then they that were in the ship came and worshipped him, saying, Of a truth thou art the Son of God.</sty>

[BODY] evidence, and in lowly reverence they expressed to him their adoring faith, saying, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Of a truth thou art the Son of God.</sty>”

[CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 15:1-20</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">OUR KING COMBATING FORMALISTS</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">1.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1"> </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">THEN came to, Jesus scribes and Pharisees, which were of Jerusalem, saying, Why do thy disciples transgress the tradition of the elders? for they wash not their hand, when they eat bread.</sty>

[BODY] When our Lord was<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>busiest his enemies assailed him. These ecclesiastics “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">of Jerusalem</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>were probably the cream of the set, and from their great reputation they reckoned upon an easy victory over the rustic preacher. Perhaps they were a deputation from headquarters, sent to confound the new Teacher. They had a question to raise, which to them may have seemed important; or possibly they pretended to think it so to answer their own purposes. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Traditions of the elders  </sty>were great things with them: to transgress these must be a crime indeed. Washing of the hands is a thing proper enough; one could wish it were oftener practiced; but to exalt it into a religious rite is a folly and a sin. These “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">scribes and Pharisee</sty>” washed their hands, whether they needed washing or not, out of a supposed zeal to be rid of any particle that might render them ceremonially unclean. Our Lord’s disciples had so far entered into Christian liberty that they did not observe the rabbinical tradition: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">they wash not their hands when they eat bread.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Why should they wash if their hands were clean? Tradition had no power over their consciences. No man has any more right to institute a new duty than to neglect an old one. The issuing of commands is for the King alone. Yet these religionists enquire why the Lord’s disciples break a law which was no law. It will be well if our opponents are unable to bring against us any worse charge than this

--- PAGE 240 ---


[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">3.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But he answered and said unto them, Why do ye also transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?</sty>

[BODY] “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">He answered</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>their question by asking them another. This was a very usual way with our Lord, and we may often imitate him in discussions with captious persons. Our Lord turns a blaze of light upon them by the question — <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Why do ye transgress the commandment of God by your tradition?  </sty>What is a “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">tradition</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>when compared with a “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">commandment</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">?</sty> What is a tradition when it is in conflict with a commandment? What are <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">elders  </sty>in<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>comparison with GOD?<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Our Lord knew best how to handle these messengers of the evil powers. His question carried the war into their own territory, and turned their boastful assault into utter rout.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">4-6.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">  For God commanded, saying, Honor thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death. But ye say, Whosoever shall say to his father or his mother, It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; and honor not his father or his mother, he shall be free. Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by tradition.</sty>

[BODY] Our Lord explains his question, and lays home his accusation. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">God  </sty>had bound the son and daughter to honor the parent; and this unquestionably included rendering to father and mother such help as they might need. From this duty there could be no escape without breaking the plain command of God. It was always right, by the law of nature, to be grateful to parents; and by the law of Moses it was always a deadly sin to revile them. In Exodus 21:17 we read: “He that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death.” Father and mother are to be had in reverence, and cherished with love; and the precept which ordains this, is called “the first commandment with promise.” There could be no mistake as to the meaning of the divine law, yet the base teachers of the period had invented a method of excusing men from the performance of so obvious a duty.

[BODY] These wretched tradition - lovers taught that if a man cried, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Corban! A gift</sty>”; and thus nominally set apart for God what his parents sought of him, he must not afterwards give it to them. If in anger, or even in pretense, he

--- PAGE 241 ---

[BODY] placed what was requested by father or mother under a ban he became <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">free</sty> from the obligation to aid his parents. It is true he was not required by the Rabbis to carry out his vow, and actually give the money or the goods to God; but as he had compromised the sacred name, he must on no account hand over the gift to his parents. So that a hasty word would loose any child from his duty to aid his father or his mother; and then he might pretend that he I was very sorry for having said it, but that his conscience would not permit him to break the ban. Vile hypocrites! Advocates of the devil! Was ever device more shallow? Yet thus they “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">made the commandment of God of  </sty>one<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>effort.”

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">7, 8.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">  Ye hypocrites, well did Esaias prophesy of you, saying, This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoreth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.</sty>

[BODY] Right well did they deserve the name which the indignant Savior fixed upon them: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Ye hypocrites.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>They were agitated about hands unwashed, and yet laid their foul hands upon God’s most holy law. The prophetic words of Isaiah were indeed descriptive of them: he had pictured them to the life. Theirs was mouth-religion, lip-homage, and that only. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Their heart</sty> never approached the Lord at all.

[BODY] Thus, our Lord gave his opponents Scripture instead of tradition: he broke their wooden weapons with the sword of the Spirit. Holy Scripture must be our weapon against the Church of traditions: nothing will overthrow Rome but the Word of the Lord.

[BODY] When quoting from the prophecy of Isaiah, our blessed Lord not only used a translation, but he gave the sense freely; thus rebuking the mere word-chopping of the Rabbis. They could count the letters of a sacred book, and yet utterly miss its meaning: he gave the soul and spirit of the inspired utterance. Jesus insisted upon heart-worship, and said nothing as to the matter of washing or not washing the hands before eating bread. That was too paltry a point for him to dwell upon.

--- PAGE 242 ---


[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">9.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.</sty>

[BODY] Religion based on human authority is worthless; we must <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">worship  </sty>the true God in the way of his own appointing, or we do not worship him at all. Doctrines and ordinances are only to be accepted when the divine Word supports them, and they are to be accepted for that reason only. The most punctilious form of devotion is <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">vain worship,  </sty>if it is regulated by man’s ordinance apart from the Lord’s own command.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">10.</sty> <sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And he called the multitude, and said unto them, Hear, and understand.</sty>

[BODY] He turns to the common throng, among whom he had wrought his miracles of love. He <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">called the multitude  </sty>and bade them “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">hear, and understand.</sty>” It looks as if he would say by his actions that he would rather teach the ignorant peasants than those false-hearted scribes and Pharisees. He had more hope of being understood by the ignorant multitude than by educated men who had so wretchedly enslaved their judgments by following worthless traditions. The appeal of the gospel is from the doctors to the people. These last have more common sense and honesty than the former; yet even these need the exhortation, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Hear, and understand.</sty>”

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">11.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man.</sty>

[BODY] Here is something for the crowd to think over, and for the Pharisees to chew upon. It would be a riddle to many, and a surprise to all. Preeminently it would be a staggering statement for formalists. Religionists of the day placed the chief point of morals in meats and drinks, but the Lord Jesus declared that it lay in thoughts and acts. The Pharisees had now a string to harp upon, since harp they would: this saying would afford a text for malicious comment for many a day. They had sought to lay hold upon a sentence which they could use as an accusation, and in this case he gave them one which they might quote with that design if they dared to do so. It was diametrically opposed to their teaching, and yet it

--- PAGE 243 ---

[BODY] was not easy to meet its keen edge, or withstand its singular force.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">12.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then came his disciples, and said unto him, Knowest thou that the Pharisees were offended, after they heard this saying</sty>

[BODY] The disciples evidently thought more of offending <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the Pharisees  </sty>than their Master did. He knew that they would be <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">offended,  </sty>and thought it no calamity that they should be. He placed his remarkable aphorism in their way, that they might find themselves balked and gravelled by it. They had come to him in a fawning manner, desiring to catch him in his speech: he was disgusted with their hypocrisy, and by this staggering statement he unmasked them, and they came out in their true colors. They could not further conceal their hate: henceforth they could not entrap the disciples by their professions of friendliness.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">13.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.</sty>

[BODY] If men are themselves an offense, they deserve to be offended. If these professed teachers of God’s mind cavil at God’s Son, they deserve no quarter; but it is right and wise to treat them to truth which shall annoy them. A good gardener is careful to uproot weeds as well as to water plants. Our Lord’s sententious utterance operated like a hoe to uproot these men from their religious profession; and he meant that it should do so. But what a solemn word is this! If our religion is not wholly of God it will come to an end, and that end will be destruction. No matter how fair the flower, if the <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Father hath not planted  </sty>it, its<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>doom is sealed: it shall not be pruned, but “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">rooted up.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Those whom the truth uproots are uprooted indeed.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">14.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Let them alone: they be blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.</sty>

[BODY] He turned from them as unworthy of further notice, saying<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>“<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Let them alone.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>There was no need for the disciples to combat the Pharisees, they would be uprooted in the natural order of things by the inevitable consequences of their own course. Both themselves and their dupes would

--- PAGE 244 ---

[BODY] “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">fall into the ditch</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>of error and absurdity; and ultimately come to utter destruction. In every case it is so: when the bigoted teacher leads the ignorant disciple, they must both go wrong. The same is the case with every form of spiritual blindness in those who lead the thought of a period, and in those who follow their erroneous guidance. The philosophic unbelief of this age is blind with self-conceit, and fearful is the ditch towards which it is hastening. Alas! its teachers are carrying precious souls with them into the ditch of Atheism and anarchy.

[BODY] O Lord, suffer us not to be despairing as to the present ascendancy of false doctrine. In patience may we possess our souls! We cannot make either the blind leaders or their blind followers see the ditch before them; but it is there all the same, and their fall is certain. Thou alone canst open the eyes of the blind, and we trust that this miracle of grace will be wrought by thee.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">15.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then answered Peter and said unto him, Declare unto us this parable.</sty>

[BODY] The saying, which Peter calls a parable, was spoken to the multitude, and then were bidden to understand it; but assuredly they did not comprehend it, for even the College of Apostles failed to grapple with it. Peter, as spokesman, did well to go at once to the fountain-head and humbly say, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Declare unto us this parable.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>He that uttered the dark saying could best interpret it.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">16.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And Jesus said, Are ye also yet without understanding?</sty>

[BODY] Of course the Pharisees would hate the light, and so refuse to see the spiritual truth which our Lord had set before them in so forcible a fashion. Nor was it wonderful that the crowd should be too ignorant to see the divine meaning of the compact sentence. But should not the chosen twelve have had clearer insight? After all their Lord’s teaching, were they “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">yet without understanding</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Should they not have reached the inner sense of their Lord’s utterance? Alas, how often have we been in a like state! How pertinently might the question be put to us, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Are ye also yet without understanding?</sty>”

--- PAGE 245 ---


[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">17.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Do not ye yet understand, that whatsoever entereth in at the mouth goeth into the belly, and is cast out into the draught?</sty>

[BODY] After years of the Master’s teaching, are we still unable to grasp an elementary truth? Can we not discern between physical and spiritual defilement? Food does not touch the soul: it passes through the body, but it does not enter the affections, or the understanding, And therefore does not defile a man. That which is eaten is material substance, and does not come into contact with the moral sense. This is clear enough to any unprejudiced mind. Meat passes through every passage of the bodily frame, from its entrance <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">at the mouth,  </sty>its<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>passage through the bowels, to its ultimate expulsion; but it bears no relation to the mental and spiritual part of our being; and it is there only that real defilement can be caused.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">18. </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart, and they defile the man.</sty>

[BODY] The<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>outcomings of the mind have sprung from the soul of the man, and have a moral character about them: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Words, and the thoughts which wear words as their garments, and the acts which are the embodiment of words; these are of the man himself, and these <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">defile  </sty>him. If the mind or heart had nothing to do with an act, it would no more pollute a man than the food which he swallows and ejects. Because acts and words come not from the mouth only, but from the soul, they are of far more importance than meats and drinks. Of course, defilement comes to a man when he is guilty of gluttony and drunkenness; yet this is not because of the mere meat or drink, but because the taking of them to excess is the exercise of unbridled appetite, and this also grows by that which gratifies it.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">19.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies.</sty>

[BODY] What a list! What must that heart be out of which so many evils pour forth! These are the bees: what must the hive be! “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Evil thoughts</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>or reasonings, such as these Pharisees had been guilty of. “Modern thought”

--- PAGE 246 ---

[BODY] is a specimen of these evils; it comes from the heart rather than from the head. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Murders</sty>” begin not with the dagger, but with the malice of the soul. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Adulteries and fornications</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>are<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>first gloated over in the heart before they are enacted by the body. The heart is the cage from whence these unclean birds fly forth. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Thefts</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>also are born in the heart: a man would not wrongfully take with the hand if he had not wrongfully desired with the heart. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">false witness</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>or<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>lying and slander: this, too, first ferments in the heart, and then its venom is spit out in the conversation. He that utters “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">blasphemies</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>against his Maker shows a very black heart: how could he fall into such a needless, useless vice, unless his inmost soul had been steeped in rebellion against the Lord? [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">20.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">These are the thing. which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man.</sty>

[BODY] They not only come from a defiled nature, but they still further <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">defile the man</sty>. Thus had the Savior proved his aphorism. The things from within evidently, are of a most defiling character, and make a man unfit for communion with God, and for the performance of holy duties; but the neglect of having water poured on the hands cannot be in the least comparable thereto. Yet those who had no repentance of polluting sins were struck with horror at a man’s eating a piece of bread <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">with unwashen hands</sty>

[BODY] Blessed Master, wash me within, and save me from the defilements of corrupt nature! Suffer me not to make outward forms my trust, but in the hidden parts purify thou me!

[CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 15:21-28</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">OUR KING AND THE WOMAN OF CANAAN</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">21.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then Jesus went thence, and departed into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">22.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil.</sty>

[BODY] were of the same country as his disciples. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">23.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But he answered her not a word. And his disciples came and besought him, saying, Send her away; for she crieth after us.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">26.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But he answered and said, It is not meet to take the children’s bread, and to cast it to dogs.</sty>

[BODY] Of course privileges must not be given to those who have no right to them, nor must reserved boons be wasted upon the unworthy. The blessing sought is as bread for children, and the Canaanites were no more members of the chosen family than so many dogs. Their heathen character made

[BODY] them like dogs as to uncleanness. For generations they had known no more of the true God than the dogs which roam the streets. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">28.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then Jesus answered and said unto her, O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt. And her daughter was made whole from that very hour.</sty>

[CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 15:29-39</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">THE KING GIVES ANOTHER BANQUET</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">29.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And Jesus departed from thence, and came nigh unto the sea of Galilee; and went up into a mountain, and sat down there.</sty>

His <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">giving thanks at an  </sty>outdoor meal should teach us not to eat without thanksgiving. The <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">breaking  </sty>teaches that there must be expenditure of talent, and that there should be a crumbing down of truth to suit human mouths. His giving the provision into many hands shows that nothing is to be retained in store, but all must be distributed among the many. Our Lord Jesus again honored <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">his disciples</sty> by making them the servitors by whom he reached the multitude. Lord, use us: for if we have neither loaf nor fish, we have grilling hands.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">37.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the broken meat that was left seven baskets full.</sty>

[BODY] The feast was carried out in a manner so orderly, and with provision so bountiful, that all ate to satisfaction: even little children had their bread and fish. The remainder, the <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">broken food,  </sty>was too good to waste, and so it was taken up in baskets for future use. The God of abundance is yet the God of frugality. We. want not, but also we waste not. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Baskets  </sty>are always to be had: the difficulty is to fill them. Here the baskets corresponded to the number of the loaves; in the former banquet they corresponded to the number of the apostles. The blessing which rewards service may bear a relation to the workers or to the original supply which they contributed, according to the manner of comparison. In both cases of feeding the multitude, that which was in store after use was greater than that which was at first possessed. The more we give the more we have. May not some of us be poor because we have given so little away? Might not the most gifted have had more gifts by this time if they had unselfishly laid out what hat they have for the good of others?

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">38.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And they that did eat were four thousand men, beside women and children.</sty>

[BODY] Here is no desire to swell out the number, to make the wonder greater. In

--- PAGE 257 ---

[BODY] some religious statistics the tale would be soon told if the <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">women and children  </sty>were left out, for they are the bulk of the attendants. In the Bible we find the people counted by the number of the males, and Matthew when he took taxes was accustomed so to levy them: that plan is followed here There is no reason why the women and children should be omitted in our enumerations nowadays, since the whole method of census taking has been altered, and both sexes are now included. As the men were the greatest eaters, and the most conspicuous persons, they are counted; and though the rest of the guests were not numbered they were all nourished, which is the main matter.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">39.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And he sent away the multitude, and took ship, and came into the coasts of Magadala.</sty>

[BODY] Our Lord was ever earnest to send the crowds home: he desired not to detain them from their daily labor. He does not want them to attend him as a guard of honor, or as enthusiastic processionists: he speeds away from their praises. <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">He took ship.  </sty>Like a shuttle through the loom, he crosses and recrosses the lake. O Lord Jesus, I would traverse the sea of life with thee as my pilot, owner, and captain!

[CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 16:1-4</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">THE KING AND HIS CHOSEN SIGN.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">1.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1"> </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">THE Pharisees also with the Sadducees come, and tempting desired him that he would shew them, a sign from, heaven</sty>

[BODY] The King is again met by his foes. Two sects, which were violently opposed to each other, unite their forces against him. It is the way of the wicked to become friends when seeking the overthrow of the kingdom of heaven.

[BODY] On this occasion they come not with a question, but with the old demand for a sign. Was it not a practical ignoring of all his previous works of power? Too often we also have fallen into the weakness of asking a new token of divine love, thus undervaluing former favors. If the evidence we have already received of our Lord’s grace and power is not enough, when will our doubts be ended?

[BODY] In this demand for a sign, our Lord’s foes were <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">tempting him.  </sty>Did the temptation lie in urging him to seek his own glory by some ostentatious display of power, for which there would be no real need? [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">2, 3.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">  He answered and said unto them, When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red. [BODY] They could prognosticate the weather by certain signs, and our Lord Jesus mentions the weather-tokens of Palestine; yet they could not read the plainer and more plentiful warnings of the near future. Weather-signs are doubtful; but there were moral and spiritual tokens around them which could hardly be misunderstood if they would only consider them. Each country has its own sky warnings, and those of Palestine differ from those of England; but the signs of the times are the same in all lands. Our Lord singled out an instance of their supposed weather-wisdom: the same sign which, in the evening, was a token of <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">fair weather,  </sty>was, in the morning, a mark of <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">foul weather.  </sty>They were able to draw nice distinctions on the variable condition of “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the face of the sky:</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>why could they not “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">discern the signs of the times?</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>They could have seen, if they had chosen to do so, that all the prophecies were one in declaring that the date of Messiah’s appearing had arrived; and they could also have observed that every event was fulfilling those prophecies; but they were false at heart, and would not see, and yet cried out for a sign. Signs were all around them, and yet they repeated the parrot cry “Show us a sign.” Most justly our Lord was indignant with them, and upbraided them, using the justly severe words, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">O ye hypocrites!</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Today the men who want more evidences of the supernatural deserve a similar denunciation.

[BODY] Lord, do not allow any of us to be blind to the heavenly signs, — thy cross, thy resurrection, thy Word, thy Spirit, and thy work of grace, Teach us carefully <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">to  </sty>“<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">discern</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>these things as being in very deed the abiding “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">signs of the times.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Even in the growing coldness of the church, and the abounding iniquity of the world, let us see the tokens of thine Advent, and stand waiting and watching for thy long promised appearing.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">4.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">A wicked and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given unto it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas. And he left them, and departed.</sty>

[BODY] It was not lack of evidence, but the sad depravity of their minds, which set them upon <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">seeking after a sign;  </sty>and therefore the Lord would not satisfy their unhealthy cranny. [BODY] Our Lord repeats his former answer: he will give them no other. In the compass of the Old Testament there is no fuller sign of our Lord than Jonah. [CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 16:5-12</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">THE KING MISUNDERSTOOD BY HIS OWN</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">5.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And when his disciples were come to the other side, they had forgotten to take bread.</sty>

[BODY] They had <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">forgotten  </sty>to victual their boat. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">6.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then Jesus said unto them, Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.</sty>

[BODY] He used a parabolic expression, which they would readily have understood, had not their minds been already absorbed by their lack of bread. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">7.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And they reasoned among themselves, saying, It is because we have taken no bread.</sty>

[BODY] Their thoughts ran along the low material level from leaven to <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">bread.  </sty>Did they imagine that he forbade their borrowing leaven from the Pharisees when they began to make a batch of bread? When a number of hungry men are together, is it not very natural that they should look at everything with hungry eyes? Yes, it is natural; and it is not natural to men to be spiritual. We need to pray that we may not <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">reason among ourselves  </sty>after the same groveling fashion, when we come into a little need.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">8-10.</sty> <sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Which when Jesus perceived, he said unto them O ye of little faith, why reason ye among yourselves, because ye have brought no bread? [BODY] Want of faith made them thus dull and carnal. Want of bread would not have troubled them if they had possessed more grace. [BODY] How foolish they were, but how like we are to them! We seem to learn nothing. [BODY] as they were. How our mind dwells on the bread which we are wanting, and how readily it forgets former times when all such wants were abundantly supplied! The <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">many baskets  </sty>which were so amply filled by former providences were the disciples’ own share and store, and therefore they ought not to have forgotten the miraculous festivals. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">11. </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">How is it that ye do not understand that I spake it not to you concerning bread, that you should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees?</sty>

--- PAGE 264 ---

[BODY] opposition against him. To this day these two forms of evil are ever working, either secretly or openly, and we have need to beware of them at all times. It is well to understand this, and both purge out the old leaven of Pharisaism, and keep out the new leaven of Sadduceeism. Self-righteousness and carnal reasoning must alike be cast out. [CENTERED_H2] <sty c="0000d4" i="0" b="0">CHAPTER 16:13-28</sty>

[CENTERED] <sty c="006411" i="0" b="1">THE KING ALONE WITH HIS FRIENDS</sty>

[BODY] The assembly which Christ gathers he builds together; for he says, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">I will build my church.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>He<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>builds on a firm foundation: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Upon this rock I will build.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>What Jesus builds is his own: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">my</sty> church.” He makes his rock-founded building into a stronghold, against which the powers of evil lay continual siege, but all in vain; for “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">the gates of hell shall not prevail against it</sty>.”

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">19.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And I will gave unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven..</sty>

[BODY] The new kingdom would not be all-comprehensive, like Noah’s ark; but would have its dove and its keys. For practical purposes the people of

--- PAGE 269 ---

[BODY] God would need discipline, and the power to receive, reinse, retain, or exclude members. Of these keys our Lord says to Peter, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Foremost among the apostles, Peter used those keys at Pentecost, when he let three thousand into the church; in Jerusalem, when he shut out Ananias and Sapphira; and at the house of Cornelius, when he admitted the Gentiles. Our Lord committed to his church power to rule within herself for him; not to set up doors, but to open or shut them: not to make laws, but to obey them and see them obeyed. Peter, and those for whom he spoke, became the stewards of the Lord Jesus in the church, and their acts were endorsed by their Lord. Today the Lord continues to back up the teaching and acts of his sent servants, those Peters who are pieces of the one Rock. The judgments of his Church, when rightly administered, have his sanction so as to make them valid. The words of his sent servants, spoken in his name, shall be confirmed of the Lord, and shall not be, either as to promise or threatening, a mere piece of rhetoric. When he was here on earth our Lord himself personally admitted men into the select circle of disciples; but on the eve of his departure he gave to their leading spirit, and thus to them also, the power to admit others to their number, or to dismiss them when found unworthy. Thus was the church or assembly constituted, and endowed with internal administrative authority. We cannot legislate, but we may and must administer the ordinances and statutes of the Lord; and what we do rightly in carrying out divine law in the church on earth is ratified by our Lord in heaven. A church would be a mere sham, and its acts a solemn farce, if the great Head of the Church did not sanction all that is done according to his statute-book.

[BODY] We need not at any length deal with the claims of the Pope of Rome. Even if Peter had been made the head of the church, how would that affect the bishop of Rome? As well say that the Cham of Tartary is the successor of Peter, as make that claim for an Italian Pontiff. No unsophisticated reader of his Bible sees any trace of Popery in this passage. The wine of Romanism is not to be pressed out of this cluster.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">20.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then charged he his disciples that they should tell no man that he was Jesus the Christ.</sty>

--- PAGE 270 ---

[BODY] As yet they were to be silent as to our Lord’s highest claims, for fear the people should in rash zeal set him up as king by force of arms. It was dangerous to tell such an ill-instructed multitude what they would be sure to misunderstand and misuse. The command <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">to tell no  </sty>man must have sounded very strangely in the disciples’ ears. It was no business of theirs to discover the reason of their Lord’s orders; it was enough for them to do as he bade them. We are under no such embargo, and therefore we will tell to all that our Lord is the Savior, the Anointed of God, or, as he has himself worded it<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">,  </sty>“<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Jesus the Christ.</sty>”

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">21.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">From that time forth began Jesus to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes</sty>, <sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">and be killed, and be raised again the third day.</sty>

[BODY] The Church or Assembly being now actually arranged, and treated as a fact, our Lord began to prepare his disciples for the time when, as an associated body, they would have to act alone, because he would be taken from them. Their first great trial would be his death, of which he had spoken darkly before. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">From that time forth began Jesus to shew unto his disciples</sty>” his death more plainly. He mentions the gathering together of his foes: “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">elders and chief priests and scribes</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>will eagerly unite. The most of them were wisely silent in their sadness, yet there was one who had far too bold a tongue.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">22.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then Peter took him, and began to rebuke him, saying, Be it far from thee, Lord: this shall not be unto thee.</sty>

[BODY] Peter could not be trusted as steward or major-domo. He takes too much upon himself. See, how great he is! He half fancies that he is the master. He loved his Lord so well that he could not bear to hear of his being killed,

--- PAGE 271 ---

[BODY] and he would gladly stop him from talking upon a subject so terribly sad. He thinks the Lord is morbid, and is attaching more importance to the opposition of the Pharisees than it deserves. Therefore he gets the Lord alone, and chides him. The words are very strong<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">:  </sty>“<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Peter took him, and began to rebuke him.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>He meant to be his Lord’s candid friend, and at the same time to maintain towards him that respectful bearing which would be becoming in his follower; but evidently he took too much on himself when he ventured to rebuke his Lord. He could see in our Lord’s death nothing but ruin to the cause, and therefore he felt it must not be. He implored the mercy of heaven to forbid so dire a catastrophe. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Be it far from thee, Lord.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>It must not, cannot fall out as Jesus had prophesied. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">This shall not be unto thee.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>He<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>would even drive such an idea out of our Lord’s mind. Should we not have done the same, had we been there, if we had been as much concerned for the honor of our Lord as Peter was? Should we not have been horror-stricken at the idea that such a One as he should be put to a cruel death? Might we not have vowed in terrible earnest, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">This shall not be unto thee  </sty>“<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">?</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">23.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">But he turned, and said unto Peter, Get thee behind me, Satan: thou art an offense unto me: for thou savorest not the thing that be of God, but those that be of men.</sty>

[BODY] Our Lord was superior to the temptation which grew out of the very love of his friend. He would remain no longer aside with Peter: <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">he turned  </sty>away from<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>him. He spied out the hindrance, and said, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Thou art an offense unto me</sty>.” His dearest friend was his direst foe when he would put him off from his life-work The devil thought to succeed through our Lord’s newly appointed foreman; but Jesus made short work of the temptation: he threw the stone out of the road, and cast it behind him, so that he could not be stumbled. The pith of the error was that Peter looked at things from the point of view of human honor and success, and not from that grand standpoint in which the glory of God in the salvation of men swallows up everything.

--- PAGE 272 ---


[BODY] A marvel is here. A man may know what only the Father can reveal, and yet he may not <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">savor the things, that be of God.  </sty>Unless he accepts the sacrifice of the Lord Jesus, he has no savor for divine things. He who does not heartily rejoice in the atonement does not discern that sweet savor of rest which the Lord God perceives in the great sacrifice, and therefore he has no fellowship in the things that be of God. He knows not the taste, the aroma, the essence of spiritual things; and however much he may honor Jesus in words, he is an enemy, yea, a real Satan towards the true Christ, whose very substance is his work as our atoning sacrifice. Those who at this day revile the substitutionary sacrifice of our Lord, are fonder of the things <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">that be of men  </sty>than those <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">that be of God</sty>. They are loud in their claim to be great philanthropists; but sound theologians they are not.Eumanitarians they may be; but divines they cannot be. They may be the friends of man; but they are not the servants of God. How sorrowfully do we write these words when we think of the many preachers to whom they apply!

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">24.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.</sty>

[BODY] As our Lord, to fulfill his destiny, must sacrifice himself, so also must every one who would be his follower. [BODY] He had told them of <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">his cross</sty>; now he tells them of their own crosses. They might now choose again whether they could and would follow him. With their increased information as to his destiny, the question was again set before them, whether they would follow or forsake him. If they did continue to be his followers, it must be as cross-bearers and self-deniers. Nor are the terms altered in these days. Do we accept them? Can we keep step in the long procession of crosscarriers, or will we fall in with the spirit of the age, and say fine things about Jesus, while we deny his

--- PAGE 273 ---

[BODY] substitutionary sacrifice, and shirk the personal self - denial which he demands? Our own wisdom, if it leads us to think lightly of “the precious blood”, must be utterly denied and even abhorred.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">25. </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it,</sty>

[BODY] Now they were to practice the doctrine he had taught them before. They could only <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">save  </sty>their<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>real selves by the loss of this present life; but if they settled it in their own minds that they must first and foremost save their outer life, it would be at the expense of their truest being. To tell them plainly of this was honest dealing on our Lord’s part; and it argued well for the disciples that they still remained faithful to him. Alas! there was one even of the chosen twelve who probably at this very moment was scheming how he could continue to keep the bag, and yet could ultimately escape from the consequences of his Master’s demand.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">26.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?</sty>

[BODY] If he loses his real life, how can he profit, even if the world be his? The true gain or loss is a gain or loss of life. All external things are trifles compared with that life. Even now, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">What is a man profited?</sty>” He has no real life in Christ, and what is all else that he may possess? What but a painted pageantry with which he is amusing his soul upon the brink of hell? As to the world to come, there is no question. To lose eternal life is overwhelming loss indeed.

[BODY] Nothing can be compared with eternal life. The soul’s value cannot be estimated by ordinary reckonings. Worlds on worlds were a poor price. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">What shall a man give in exchange for his soul</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Barter is out of the question. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">28.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">1.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1"> AND after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, and was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun and his raiment was white as the light</sty>

[BODY] Were these “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">six days</sty>,” a week’s quiet interval, in which our Lord prepared himself for the singular transaction upon the “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">mountain apart</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">?</sty> Did the little company of three know from one Sabbath to another that such an amazing joy awaited them? The three were elect out of the elect, and favored to see what none else in all the world might behold. Doubtless our Lord had reasons for his choice, as he has for every choice he makes; but he does not unveil them to us. The same three beheld the agony in the garden; perhaps the first sight was necessary to sustain their faith under the second.

[BODY] The name of the “high mountain” can never be known; for those who knew the locality have left no information. Tabor, if you please; Hermon, if you prefer it. No one can decide. It was a lone and lofty hill.

[BODY] While in prayer, the splendor of the Lord shone out. His face, lit up with its<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>own inner glory, became a sun; and all his dress, like clouds irradiated by that sun became white as the light itself “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">He was transfigured before them</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">:  </sty>he alone was the center of what they saw. [BODY] The transfiguration occurred but once: special views of the glory of Christ are not enjoyed every day. Our highest joy on earth is to see Jesus. There

--- PAGE 277 ---

[BODY] can be no greater bliss in heaven; but we shall be better able to endure the exceeding bliss when we have laid aside the burden of this flesh.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">3.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.</sty>

Saints long departed still live; live in their personality; are known by their names; and enjoy near access to Christ. It is a great joy to holy ones to be with Jesus: they find it heaven to be where they can talk with him. The heads of former dispensations conversed with the Lord as to his decease, by which a new economy I would be ushered in. After condescending so long to his ignorant followers, it must have been a great relief to the human soul of Jesus to talk with two master-minds like those of Moses and Elijah. What a sight for the apostles, this glorious trio! They “appeared unto them”, but they “talked with him”: the object of the two holy ones was not to converse with apostles, but with their Master. Although saints are seen of men, their fellowship is with Jesus.

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">5. </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">While he yet spake, behold a bright cloud overshadowed them: and behold a voice out of the cloud, which said, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear ye him.</sty>

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">6.</sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">  And when the disciples heard it, they fell on their face and were sore afraid.</sty>

[BODY] Yes, the voice overcame them. [BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">7.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And Jesus came and touched them, and said, Arise, and be not afraid.</sty>

The voice from heaven casts down; but the word from Jesus is, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Arise</sty>.” The Father’s voice made them sore afraid, but Jesus says, “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">Be not afraid.</sty>”<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>Glorious God, how much we bless thee for the Mediator!

[BODY] <sty c="000000" i="0" b="1">8.</sty><sty c="000000" i="1" b="1">  </sty><sty c="800000" i="1" b="1">And when they had lifted up their eyes, they saw no man, save Jesus only.</sty>

[BODY] Closed were their eyes, because of “the too transporting light”; and they dared not open them till they felt the touch of Jesus. Then <sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">they lifted up their eyes.  </sty>What<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">  </sty>did they see?

[BODY] Moses, and Elias, and the exceeding brightness had all gone, and they had come back to the common-places of their life with Jesus. “<sty c="800000" i="1" b="0">They saw no</sty>
